topic: Why a song gets stuck in your head
title: Why That Song Won't Leave Your Head
voiceover: Why is that song stuck in your head? Scientists call it an earworm, and in one Finnish survey over ninety percent of people said they get one weekly. Studies suggest earworms tend to be fairly fast, with simple, easy-to-sing melodies, often triggered by recent listening, stress, or a memory cue. Songs you've heard a lot recently are prime candidates. Your brain's auditory and memory systems keep replaying the loop, even when you aren't trying. Researchers still don't fully understand why some songs stick and others don't. One small experiment found that chewing gum reduced earworms, likely because it interferes with silently singing along. Engaging, moderately tricky puzzles may help too. Try both. Tomorrow: the sneaky first number stores show you, on purpose, before the real price.

description: Earworms often follow recent listening, stress, or a memory cue, and tend to have simple, easy-to-sing melodies. A small experiment found that chewing gum can reduce them. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Beaman, Powell & Rapley (2015), 'Want to block earworms from conscious awareness? B(u)y gum!', Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology.
accuracy_note: The 90%+ weekly figure comes from a survey of Finnish adults (Liikkanen, 2012) and may not generalize. Song traits (fairly fast tempo, simple/common melodic shapes) follow Jakubowski et al. (2016). The chewing-gum finding comes from small lab experiments and shouldn't be treated as a guaranteed cure; the research on why particular songs become earworms is still developing.
